practicalQuestion: Which criteria should a physical therapist prioritize when deciding whether a collegiate field- or court-sport athlete is ready to progress from controlled rehabilitation drills to a higher-intensity field or court session?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete in late-stage lower-extremity rehabilitation
decisionContext.phase: Planned progression from controlled drills to higher-intensity individual work
decisionContext.outcome: Make a defensible next-step progression decision while monitoring response
decisionContext.constraints: De-identified scenario; no diagnosis or clearance request; available evidence is primarily group-level

evidenceConfidence.rationale: The sources consistently advocate criterion-based, multi-domain progression with attention to how the knee or tissues respond to load. The pack rests on one uncontrolled case series (100 male soccer players, professional and amateur), one single-player case study, one expert-developed ankle algorithm whose effectiveness its authors say remains to be evaluated, and one narrative review. All are from soccer and each covers a specific injury (ACL reconstruction, lateral ankle sprain, hamstring strain). No source compares progression criteria or validates thresholds for the step from controlled drills to higher-intensity individual field work. The ankle algorithm authors state that criteria are lacking for football-specific stress progression, which is the stage closest to this decision.

dimensions.sourceReview: Four relevant sources: a case series of 100 male soccer players (professional and amateur) after ACL reconstruction, a case study of one elite male soccer player after ACL reconstruction, a clinical commentary presenting an ankle sprain rehabilitation algorithm for professional soccer, and a narrative review on hamstring strains in football. All claims are checked against original source text.
dimensions.directness: Moderately direct. Two sources describe on-field rehabilitation progression after ACL reconstruction, and one defines level-to-level entry criteria after ankle sprain, though its authors say criteria are lacking for the football-specific stage. None tests whether a given criterion predicts a safe progression.
dimensions.consistency: Consistent on direction: progression should be criterion-based, multi-domain, and responsive to tissue reaction. Sources differ in how much they rely on fixed pass or fail thresholds, and several thresholds are experience-based.
dimensions.transferability: Limited. The populations are male or professional soccer players with specific injuries, and the ACL case series authors state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players. Transfer to collegiate athletes of either sex in other field or court sports, and to an unspecified lower-extremity injury, is uncertain.

bottomLine.text: The sources advocate criterion-based progression that combines patient-reported status, a clinical examination, functional performance tests, and how the knee and soft tissues responded to recent loads, but none tests whether this approach produces safer progressions. Specific thresholds in this pack are injury-specific, partly set from practitioner experience, and not validated for this decision. The ankle algorithm authors also note that criteria are lacking for the football-specific stage that most resembles a higher-intensity field session.

actions.title: Option A: Use a multi-domain pass or fail gate
actions.text: One option is an ankle sprain algorithm in professional soccer. It requires passing three assessments before the next level: a level-dependent patient-reported score, a standardised clinical examination, and performance tests. To enter its athletic skills level, it requires an AFS above 85/100, a passed clinical examination, and passed multidirectional hop tests, with passing defined as a limb symmetry index above 90%. High-dynamic hop tests are first done qualitatively to check movement quality and pain response. The AFS benchmarks were set from the authors' experience in accordance with the literature, the authors call the LSI debatable, and they state the algorithm's effectiveness remains to be evaluated.

actions.title: Option B: Progress on tissue response plus stage criteria
actions.text: Another option comes from a case series of 100 male soccer players after ACL reconstruction. There, stage transitions were driven by a continuous comparison of drills with how the knee and soft tissues responded to the loads, along with defined stage-specific criteria from a published 5-stage program. The program covered movement quality, physical conditioning, soccer-specific skills, and training load. The authors judged total distance not useful for progressing through on-field rehabilitation because it plateaued. Players who reached the final stage had higher return-to-competition rates (90% vs 71%), but the authors say it is unclear what drove this.

actions.title: Option C: Add field-based asymmetry data
actions.text: A third option comes from a single-player ACL case study. Its authors state that GPS-embedded inertial sensor data on stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries, in addition to usual strength and jump assessments, can be used to guide phase progression. In that case, a step impulse asymmetry coincided with knee pain and the player stopped running for a few days. The ACL case series notes that it remains unclear which GPS metrics are relevant for return-to-competition readiness or for planning on-field rehabilitation workloads.

actions.title: Option D: Tie running speed and change of direction to strength benchmarks
actions.text: In the same single-player case, after a hamstring autograft, practitioners used hamstring strength benchmarks to guide running speed: above 70% isometric strength to run above 15 km/h, above 90% to run above 20 km/h, and above 90% eccentric strength for near-maximal speeds and maximal change of direction intensities. The authors describe hamstring strength as an important but not unique criterion for speed progression. The source does not state the reference value for these percentages, and the benchmarks are tied to a hamstring graft.

actions.title: Check domain coverage, not just one test
actions.text: The ACL case study cites earlier work describing progression criteria across range of motion, strength, balance and control, and functional capacities such as jumping, landing, cutting, accelerating and decelerating. A hamstring review lists pain-free performance of high-intensity activities, restoration of strength and flexibility to pre-injury levels, and absence of compensatory movement patterns, though as return-to-play criteria. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): confirm no single domain is being used as the sole gate.

monitoring.label: Tissue and joint response after each step
monitoring.text: Track how the knee or affected tissues respond to the new loads before the next increase, as in the ACL case series. The ankle algorithm authors recommend attention to clinical responses after training during the return to ball work, and they check that swelling is not more than +1% above the previous measurement, but that threshold is ankle-specific.

monitoring.label: Field load against reference demands
monitoring.text: In the ACL case series, final-stage on-field rehabilitation loads, compared with team training demands reported in the literature, were 106% for total distance, 104% for high-intensity distance, 88% for peak speed, 110% for acceleration distance, and only 48% for deceleration distance. The authors conclude players were underprepared for deceleration demands, and that total distance was not useful for progressing. The single-player case study also found high mechanical work intensities hard to reach in individual sessions. Watch deceleration and change-of-direction exposure in particular.

monitoring.label: Asymmetry trend, if sensors are available
monitoring.text: Step impulse asymmetry from inertial sensors was used in one elite player case, where an asymmetry coincided with knee pain and a short pause in running. The authors state it can be used to guide phase progression. Treat it as a supplementary signal, not a validated cutoff.

guardrails.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians. This brief informs criteria and monitoring only and does not diagnose, prescribe, or clear an athlete.

Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): do not apply the ankle range of motion, swelling, AFS, or LSI thresholds to other injuries. They come from an ankle sprain algorithm whose effectiveness its authors say remains to be evaluated, and some were set from the authors' experience.

Completing individual field stages does not reproduce interactive demands. In soccer, some cutting, decelerating and ball movements occur only with teammates and opponents, especially during competition, and the ACL case series found on-field rehabilitation did not fully prepare players for full team training workloads. A successful individual session is not evidence of readiness for unrestricted or team work.

limitations.text: The direct evidence is a level 4 case series of 100 male soccer players after ACL reconstruction with no control group, and a case study of one elite male soccer player. Neither tests whether specific criteria predict a safe progression, and the association between reaching the final stage and return to competition has no clear cause.

The ankle algorithm is an expert-developed clinical commentary in professional soccer. Its authors frame benefit as something that might occur, supported by practical experience of feasibility, and state its effectiveness remains to be evaluated.

The ankle algorithm authors state there are no football-specific tests or criteria for football-specific stress progression, so its defined criteria stop short of the stage most like a higher-intensity field session.
The hamstring criteria come from a narrative review and describe return-to-play, not the earlier step to higher-intensity individual work.

All sources study soccer. The collegiate setting, court sports, and the athlete's specific injury are not represented, and the ACL case series authors state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players.

whatCouldChange.text: Studies that test which GPS metrics are relevant for readiness and for adjusting on-field workloads, which the ACL case series identifies as unclear.
A controlled evaluation of a criterion-based progression algorithm, which the ankle algorithm authors say is still needed.
Evidence in collegiate, female, or court-sport athletes during late-stage lower-extremity rehabilitation.

evidenceTension.text: The ankle algorithm relies on predefined pass or fail assessments with numeric cutoffs. The ACL case series drove transitions partly by observed knee and soft tissue response, and states that it remains unclear which GPS metrics are relevant for readiness. This is a difference in approach rather than a direct contradiction. Fixed thresholds have not been shown to outperform response-driven progression, or the reverse.

claims.text: In an ankle sprain rehabilitation algorithm for professional soccer, progression to the next level requires passing three assessments: a level-dependent patient-reported outcome score, a standardised clinical examination, and performance tests. The athlete stays at a level until each is passed.

evidence.excerpt: achieving a level-dependent score in the patient reported outcome measure, passing a standardised clinical examination, and passing performance tests
The athlete remains at a rehabilitation level until each assessment for progression to the next level is passed.

claims.text: In the same ankle sprain algorithm, the clinical examination requires less than 10 degrees side-to-side dorsiflexion difference for Levels 1 and 2 and range of motion equal to the non-injured ankle for later levels. Swelling should not exceed +1% of the previous measurement, to check for irritant reactions.

evidence.excerpt: Side to side difference in ROM should be less than 10 degrees of dorsiflexion to pass the clinical examination for Levels 1 and 2. Furthermore, ROM should be the same compared to the non-injured ankle to pass the criteria for progression to the ongoing levels.
The swelling should not be more than +1% compared to the previous measurement to check possible irritant reactions.

claims.text: To enter its athletic skills level (Level 4), the ankle sprain algorithm requires an AFS score above 85/100, a passed clinical examination, and passed hop tests (Square Hop, Crossover Hop, and a modified 6 m timed Crossover Hop).

evidence.excerpt: AFS>85/100 Pass the clinical examination Pass hop tests (Square Hop Test; Crossover Hop Test; mod. 6m-timed Crossover Hop Test)

Ultimately, the use of LSI remains debatable for assessing lateral differences in the lower limbs after injury.

claims.text: The ACL case series authors conclude that on-field rehabilitation helped prepare players for return to team training but did not fully prepare them for full team training workloads, and that players were underprepared for deceleration demands.

indicating that players are underprepared for the DEC demands of soccer after OFR.

claims.text: In the ACL case series, players who reached the final on-field stage had higher return-to-competition rates than the rest of the cohort (90% vs 71%, P = .016), but the authors state it is unclear whether workloads, level of play, or number of sessions explained this.

evidence.excerpt: Players who reached stage 5 of the OFR program (33%) had higher RTC rates compared with the rest of the cohort (90% vs 71%; P = .016).

However, it remains unclear whether increased OFR workloads enhanced physical and psychological readiness for RTC or whether it was the level of play or the number of OFR sessions that determined higher RTC rates.

assumptions: The specific lower-extremity injury is not stated, so ACL, ankle sprain, and hamstring sources were treated as indirect examples rather than injury-matched guidance.
The higher-intensity session was assumed to be individual work without opponents, consistent with the stated phase.
coverageGaps: No studies of collegiate athletes or court sports in late-stage lower-extremity rehabilitation.
No source studies female athletes for on-field progression criteria; the ACL case series authors state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players.
No comparative or validation studies showing which criteria or thresholds predict a safe step from controlled drills to higher-intensity individual field or court work.
